https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/clye17.text: Ukrainian vegetable seller targeted in 'human safari' drone attack Ukrainian vegetable seller targeted in 'human safari' drone attack Close Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared a video of a street vendor being hunted by a drone before it exploded. The man in the video verified by the BBC, 52-year-old street vegetable seller Yuriy, managed to survive the attack, but sustained shrapnel wounds and a concussion. Known by some in Ukraine as "human safari", the deployment of remotely-operated drones against civilians has often been used by Russians to terrify residents of front line areas. This particular drone attack happened in Kherson, which sits only a few miles from the front line. Russia has repeatedly denied intentionally targeting civilians. The BBC's Paul Adams reports from Kyiv. More on this story. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/09/13-ki.text: Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes overnight that killed civilians and injured many others on both sides, local authorities reported.Large-scale Russian missile strikes on Ukrainian cities have become almost routine in recent weeks, with Moscow exploiting Ukraine’s critical shortage of interceptors for the US-made Patriot systems — the sole air defence weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles.In the latest attacks, Ukrainian drones killed five people and injured two dozen others, including a four-year-old boy, in Russia’s border region of Belgorod, according to the regional administration.Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says four people were killed in the Kyiv capital region, a three-year-old boy and his grandparents, in one strike, and later another fatality was reported in a separate strike, also on civilian infrastructure.“More pressure is needed — new sanctions that will prevent Russia from producing these ballistic missiles. And our people absolutely need more protection. Anti-ballistic systems, interceptor missiles for Patriot, SAMP/T, NASAMS, and HAWK systems, as well as our F-16s,” wrote Zelenskyy in a post on the Telegram messaging app.In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, Russian missiles struck a high-rise apartment block in the Saltivskyi district, killing three people and injuring 37, according to regional head Oleh Syniehubov.At least six other deaths were reported in strikes on other frontline cities, including Sumy, Kherson and Donetsk in the eastern industrial Donbas region.Eight more people were injured in Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa after “dozens of missiles and drones” struck the city and surrounding region, according to local administration head Oleh Kiper.Ukrainian officials say 13 people were killed and approximately 90 others were injured in Russian attacks over the past 24 hours.Zelenskyy has for months lobbied other countries, especially the United States, to send Ukraine more Patriot systems, made scarcer by the Iran war, arguing they are crucial for defending civilians.Failing that, Zelenskyy wants to make Patriot ammunition in Ukraine or get approval from Elon Musk to use his Starlink satellite communications system to guide strikes inside Russia that can hit its missile launchers.Meanwhile, Kyiv has kept up long-range drone strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, as well as the country’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, and other targets deep inside Russia, sparking a fuel crisis.Russia’s defence ministry on Sunday claimed its overnight strikes hit drone warehouses in the Kharkiv region, as well as fuel depots and stores of other materiel belonging to Ukraine’s armed forces at the port of Odesa.It said its forces had shot down 153 Ukrainian drones overnight into Sunday, including over Russian-occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.In Russia's Belgorod region, authorities said Ukrainian drone strikes damaged 29 apartment blocks and five private houses, as well as administrative buildings and unspecified “commercial facilities.”Debris from Ukrainian drones also fell on two enterprises and a private home in the Russian city of Novorossiysk, mayor Andrey Kravchenko said on Sunday.A major fuel terminal is located at Novorossiysk that links Kazakhstan's oil fields to markets around the world, and which has previously been a target for Ukrainian strikes, as Kyiv looks to suffocate the Kremlin’s energy sector, which it believes to be the financial arm of its invasion.

http://www.aina.org/news/20260804115318..text: 14th World Congress of Syriac Studies Opens in Bucharest Syriac Press Posted 2026-08-04 16:53 GMT Bucharest -- The 14th World Congress of Syriac [modern Assyrian] Studies, also called Symposium Syriacum, opened on Monday at the Palace of Parliament in Bucharest, Romania, bringing together more than 400 scholars and specialists from 33 countries and 176 universities to examine the history, language, theology, and cultural heritage of one of the world's oldest Christian traditions. Held from 3 to 7 August, the international symposium is being hosted in Romania for the first time by the Levant Institute for Advanced Studies for the Culture of Peace, under the coordination of Dr. Catalin-?tefan Popa, Director-General of the institute and a researcher at the Romanian Academy's Institute for the History of Religions. Held under the theme Peace and Dialogue -- Prerequisites for the Protection of Literary and Material Heritage, the congress underscores the urgent need to preserve Syriac literary treasures, ancient manuscripts, and religious traditions that have shaped the intellectual and spiritual history of the Middle East for nearly two millennia. The opening ceremony brought together representatives of Romanian state institutions, academic bodies, and religious organizations, including officials from the Romanian Academy, the Romanian Patriarchate, the Presidency, the Government, the Senate, and the Chamber of Deputies. A central figure at the congress is Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East Mar Awa III Royel who is scheduled to address participants on the significance of Syriac Christianity and the shared responsibility of preserving its theological and cultural legacy. Headquartered in Ankawa, Arab'ilo (Erbil), Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI), the Assyrian Church of the East is among the world's oldest Christian Churches with a history deeply rooted in the Syriac language and tradition. Patriarch Mar Awa III, who holds a PhD in Theology from the Pontifical Oriental Institute in Rome, is widely recognized for his contributions to the study and advancement of Syriac theology and spirituality. The congress features leading international scholars whose research has significantly expanded global understanding of Syriac civilization, including specialists from Yale University, the University of Hamburg, the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Princeton University, the University of Edinburgh, Durham University, and the University of Oxford. Among the invited speakers are Kevin van Bladel, Aaron Michael Butts, Françoise Briquel-Chatonnet, Valentina Duca, George Kiraz, Salam Rassi, Alberto Rigolio, Columba Stewart, Jack Tannous, and David G. K. Taylor, all internationally recognized for their contributions to the study of Syriac manuscripts, literature, theology, and the history of Christianity in the Middle East. For Assyrian communities around the world, the gathering serves as a reaffirmation of a heritage that has endured centuries of political upheaval, persecution, displacement, and demographic change. From ancient monasteries and manuscript collections to liturgical traditions and the continued use of the Assyrian language, the congress places renewed emphasis on safeguarding the cultural identity of Assyrian-speaking communities, particularly in their historic homeland of Mesopotamia. As many Assyrian Christian communities continue to face challenges related to displacement and the loss of cultural and religious sites, scholars and religious leaders participating in the Bucharest symposium are emphasizing the importance of international cooperation in protecting both the tangible and intangible heritage of the Assyrian world. (Jon Chiu/The Morning Call) Expand By Avery Folmar | afolmar@mcall.com | The Morning Call PUBLISHED: August 4, 2026 at 7:00 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... As the nation celebrates its 250th anniversary this year, a Lehigh Valley church is inviting people to look beyond the country’s well-known historical figures and events and instead explore the stories that began in their own families. The Allentown FamilySearch Center, located at 1881 Van Buren Drive in Whitehall Township, is part of an effort by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to connect people with their family histories. The church is collaborating with America250 campaign on initiatives involving service, family history and music. Through FamilySearch, people are encouraged to explore the lives of ancestors who immigrated to the United States, lived through important moments in the nation’s history and helped shape the country. The center is open to the public, regardless of religious affiliation, and its services are free. For Malva Snyder, the church’s communication director for nine local congregations, family history can help people better understand not only where they came from but also where they belong. “There’s so much available here,” Snyder said. “It really helps you to feel that sense of belonging, that sense of community, and your self-worth, knowing what your ancestors did before you.” Though it can be done from home, the FamilySearch Center offers computers with access to FamilySearch.org as well as a collection of historical books, records and other resources. Visitors also can access several subscription genealogy websites, including Ancestry, Findmypast and MyHeritage, at no cost while at the center. The center also provides something an online search can’t always offer: people who can help researchers navigate the process and point them toward resources they might otherwise overlook. Additionally, some historical records are available only through FamilySearch Centers because of agreements with the organizations that own them. The Whitehall center has a collection of family history books focused on Lehigh and Berks counties, along with resources for researching German and Austro-Hungarian ancestry. Ann Thompson, the center’s coordinator, said the resources can help people who may arrive with little more than a name or two and leave with a much deeper understanding of their family. She recalled one visitor who came in knowing only the names of their grandparents. With the help of center resources, Thompson said, the person was able to trace their family back to the 1700s in about two hours. “Our job is to show them how to do it,” Thompson said. The process has changed significantly since Thompson began working with the center. When she arrived in 1989, researchers relied on microfiche and film. Today, much of that work can be done digitally, though some records still require researchers to visit a FamilySearch Center. Thompson said the center’s resources are particularly useful for people researching ancestors from the Lehigh Valley and surrounding areas. Its collection includes local history books and older records that can be difficult to find elsewhere. For Regina Sanders, who’s been researching her family history for more than two decades, the center became a gateway to a hobby that has taken her from researching ancestors in Poland to tracing her husband’s family back to the Mayflower. A seminar at Bethlehem Area Public Library introduced Sanders to genealogy, she said. She was encouraged to visit the center and work with Thompson and other volunteers. “I started my research with my family and did many years in Poland,” Sanders said. “And then I decided to jump into my husband’s family, which goes back to the Mayflower.” Sanders said the center has helped guide her through difficult searches, including an ongoing effort to find ancestors on her Polish side who lived in an area that is now part of Ukraine. Genealogy, she said, comes with its share of dead ends, but the process has become easier as more records have moved online. “There are a lot of brick walls, and you just have to find ways to get around them,” Sanders said. The center’s connection to America250 is intended to encourage more people to begin that process, particularly by recording their own stories alongside those of their ancestors. FamilySearch’s America250 initiative encourages people to explore their family trees, preserve memories and learn how their ancestors fit into the broader story of the nation. Snyder said that effort is especially meaningful in Pennsylvania, where she’s noticed many families have remained in the same communities for generations. “I have found, in particular Pennsylvania, there are so many people here that have stayed here for generations and generations,” she said. The center hopes the America250 celebration will help more people discover the resources available in their own backyard. The Allentown FamilySearch Center is open 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Tuesdays, 7-8:30 p.m. Wednesdays, and 9 a.m. to noon Thursdays and Saturdays. It’s closed on holidays. The center is one of several FamilySearch locations serving the region, with additional centers in Reading and Pottstown. A banner hanging above the center captures the spirit of the initiative in a simple message: “Celebrate your family’s place in history during America250.” Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Most Popular Most Popular Woman, 21, killed in crash on Airport Road in Lehigh County [Updated] Woman, 21, killed in crash on Airport Road in Lehigh County [Updated] Lehigh Valley warehouse to close, affecting more than 50 workers Lehigh Valley warehouse to close, affecting more than 50 workers New Hobby Lobby to open next month in the Lehigh Valley New Hobby Lobby to open next month in the Lehigh Valley What are the best hospitals in Lehigh Valley? https://www.dw.com/en/china-cargo-ship-f.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MMqG Qingdao is one of China's largest ports [FILE APRIL 2026] Image: Imaginechina/Sipa USA/picture alliance Advertisement At least 25 people were killed and five remain missing after a fire on a cargo vessel receiving repairs at a shipyard in the northeastern Chinese port city of Qingdao, state media reported on Thursday. State broadcaster CCTV reported the vessel with 42 people on board caught fire at around 11:15 a.m. local time, and were extinguished around 2:30 p.m. (0630 UTC)." The ship was identified as the 190-metre (623-foot) long bulk carrier "Ocean Melody," which sails under a Liberian flag, state news agency Xinhua reported. Cause remains unclear Chinese President Xi Jinping issued has "important instructions" to conduct a search and rescue mission, while also calling for an investigation into anyone who could be responsible for the incident, Xinhua added. Xi said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards". It is currently unclear what could have caused the fire. The vessel was undergoing repairs at Qingdao's Beihai Shipbuilding Co, part of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), one of the world's largest shipbuilders. Oregon school shooting Six Flags reopening Katie Zacharia 'lawyer' flap 'Governor gap' races Cornell rape case latest Social Security's 2027 COLA Roller coaster tragedy Bank of America penalized French National Rally leader Jordan Bardella visits the Yad Vashem Holocaust Memorial in Jerusalem on March 26, 2025 (Jack GUEZ) Facing growing isolation over the war in Gaza, Israel is increasingly allying itself with Europe's far right, despite some parties' legacies of antisemitism. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has accused foreign critics of Israel's conduct in Gaza of fanning hate against Jews, but his government has mostly been comfortable with politicians so long as they support Israel. After a French investigative site on Monday alleged that far-right National Rally leader Jordan Bardella made derogatory remarks about Jews as a teenager, Netanyahu's minister in charge of combatting antisemitism defended him. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Amichai Chikli said that Bardella, who could become prime minister if frontrunner Marine Le Pen wins next year's presidential election, "is one of the clearest voices in Europe against Hamas". He pointed to his meetings on a visit to Israel last year with survivors of Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack, the deadliest ever against Israel which responded with its massive military campaign in Gaza. In 2000, Israel recalled its ambassador to Austria and backed an international shaming campaign after the formation of a government that included the Freedom Party, founded by former Nazis. But Netanyahu's government has moved to normalise ties with the Freedom Party. Advertisement Advertisement Chikli in September hailed a "historic turning point" after Freedom Party leader Herbert Kickl delivered a speech vowing that if in power, his government's programme would include "combatting antisemitism and fighting against anti-Zionism". - 'Kosher certificate' for far right - Israel has also courted other far-right leaders in Europe, including in Sweden, Spain and Britain, with Israeli politicians bonding over shared concerns about Muslim migration to the West. Farther afield, Israel has hailed as a watershed its relations in Latin America after the election of hard-right, pro-Israel presidents in Argentina and Colombia. Advertisement Advertisement One bridge too far, at least for now, is Germany, with Israeli officials still shunning the far-right AfD. Jeremy Issacharoff, Israel's ambassador in Berlin from 2017 to 2022, as the AfD was emerging, said that some European far-right parties were looking for ways to show they have evolved from past antisemitism. By building relations with Israel, "they get a sort of kosher certificate," Issacharoff told AFP. "I can see what they get out of it; for Israel I only see damage to its values and its international standing," he said. "Over the past three years, when you see greater criticism of Israel from the centre and the left, that creates a motivation from Israel's right-wing politicians to counterbalance that by appearing to have some elements in common," he added. Advertisement Advertisement Issacharoff said that in Germany, but also in other European countries including France and Austria, Israel should first consider how supporting the far right would impact local Jewish communities. In Britain, Jewish groups voiced alarm after Israel last year welcomed far-right provocateur Tommy Robinson and hailed his views on radical Islam. - Seeing benefit in divisions - Israeli officials have used strikingly undiplomatic language about Western leaders who criticise Israel. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar recently called the leader of Britain's hard-right Reform Party to hail his opposition to new UK sanctions on goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Advertisement Advertisement Israel at the same time denounced British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, the son of Jewish refugees, with Chikli even mocking his hairstyle. Azriel Bermant, an associate researcher at the Institute of International Relations Prague who has studied Israel's relations with Europe, said that Netanyahu's embrace of the far right was also about driving wedges within Europe. "As far as Netanyahu sees it, any countries that can support Israel and go against the European consensus, so much the better as far as he's concerned," Bermant said. He pointed to Netanyahu's relationship with Viktor Orban, Hungary's leader until he lost elections this year. Advertisement Advertisement Orban backed Israel even while critics said his campaign against George Soros, the billionaire philanthropist, tapped into antisemitic tropes. Bermant expected Israel's approach to shift if Netanyahu loses power in October 27 elections, with his rivals still likely to reach out to leaders such as Le Pen who have a chance of taking office, but not identifying Israel with the far right. One former Israeli ambassador in Europe, who asked for anonymity to preserve relationships, said he understood why Israel would not denounce Bardella, considering the possibility he and Le Pen will be leading France next year. But he said Israel also needed to be more pragmatic by not rushing to align itself with divisive figures. "One day governments will change from right to left, from left to right, and if you glue yourselves to the radical right, then you paint yourself with a certain colour," he said. sct/ris/ser/abs/axn Advertisement About Our Ads About Our Ads Advertisement Advertisement Recommended articles Housing loans granted while Burnham was mayor investigated by councillors A senior councillor says concerns have been raised about the transparency of the process to approve the loans.
